HMMs

Author

Jonathan Rodemann, Sophia Costa

Hidden Markov Models

This vignette goes over the process for getting positional data ready for HMM analysis and running the analysis using the moveHMM package.

#Load in libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(moveHMM)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(parallel)
library(circular)
## 
## Attaching package: 'circular'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     sd, var

dat <- read_csv('data/dat_HMM.csv')
## New names:
## • `` -> `...1`
## • `...2` -> `...3`
## Rows: 8436 Columns: 23
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr   (3): z, z_sd, trackstart
## dbl  (17): ...1, tag, ...3, x, y, x_sd, y_sd, nobs, k, E, Year, Month, Day, ...
## dttm  (1): ts
## date  (1): Date
## time  (1): Time
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

# Parse timestamp
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(ts = as.POSIXct(ts,
                         format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS",
                         tz = "UTC"))

head(dat)

## 2     2 34501  1194 2022-02-04 06:33:11 518861. 2778481. Y     2.69   3.05 Y    
## 3     3 34501  1195 2022-02-04 06:33:40 518861. 2778481. Y     3.02   3.36 Y

## # ℹ 13 more variables: nobs <dbl>, k <dbl>, E <dbl>, Date <date>, Time <time>,
## #   Year <dbl>, Month <dbl>, Day <dbl>, Hour <dbl>, Minute <dbl>, Second <dbl>,
## #   trackstart <chr>, track <dbl>

The model expects at least these columns: tag : individual identifier track : track number/ID for that individual’s track segment ts : timestamp string x, y : coordinates (assumed UTM/metres). If they’re lat/long, convert to projected meters first.

Interpolation of tracks to a regular time interval

Hidden Markov Models require the data to have a regular time step. Because these positions are calculated from random burst tags, we need to interpolate the tracks to a regular interval. This is the third big decision - how do you parse out the time interval to interpolate the tracks? Our suggestion is to start at twice the average burst interval of the tag to account for possible missed detections.

#store the columns needed for this step
ts_col <- "ts"
id_col <- "tag"
track_col <- "track"
x_col <- "x"
y_col <- "y"

#Create a function that interpolates the tracks from the positions. For this function to work, you need to group the data before running it into unique ID X track combinations

interpolate_track <- function(df_group, dt_seconds = 180) { #The default time of the interpolated tracks is 3 minutes, but you can change that
  # df must contain columns: ts, x, y, plus id/track identifiers
  if (nrow(df_group) < 2) return(NULL)  # can't interpolate single-point tracks
  
  tmin <- min(df_group$ts, na.rm = TRUE)
  tmax <- max(df_group$ts, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  new_times <- seq(from = tmin, to = tmax, by = dt_seconds) #sequence the track out to regular intervals based on your start and end times and the interval you identify in the function
  if (length(new_times) < 2) return(NULL)
  
  # numeric times for approx - makes math easier
  orig_t_num <- as.numeric(df_group$ts)
  new_t_num <- as.numeric(new_times)
  
  # ensure sorted by time - earliest to latest
  ord <- order(orig_t_num)
  orig_t_num <- orig_t_num[ord]
  x_orig <- df_group[[x_col]][ord]
  y_orig <- df_group[[y_col]][ord]
  
  # linear interpolation (NA handling: approx requires finite values) - takes actual points and times, then interpolates the point between the actual points based on actual times
  ok_x <- is.finite(x_orig) & is.finite(orig_t_num)
  ok_y <- is.finite(y_orig) & is.finite(orig_t_num)
  if (!any(ok_x) || !any(ok_y)) return(NULL)
  
  x_interp <- approx(x = orig_t_num[ok_x], y = x_orig[ok_x], xout = new_t_num, rule = 2)$y #The y extracts only the interpolated points
  y_interp <- approx(x = orig_t_num[ok_y], y = y_orig[ok_y], xout = new_t_num, rule = 2)$y

  tibble(
    ts = new_times, #interpolated times
    !!id_col := df_group[[id_col]][1],
    !!track_col := df_group[[track_col]][1],
    x = x_interp,
    y = y_interp
  )
}

#Now let's run it on our data!
interp_list <- dat %>%
  group_by(.data[[id_col]], .data[[track_col]]) %>%
  group_map(~ interpolate_track(.x, dt_seconds = 60), .keep = TRUE)

# Remove NULLs (tracks that couldn't be interpolated)
interp_list <- keep(interp_list, ~ !is.null(.x) && nrow(.x) > 0)

interp_df <- bind_rows(interp_list) #make dataframe
interp_df <- interp_df %>% mutate(ID = paste(tag, track, sep = "_")) #make ID column

We have our interpolated tracks! As you can see, we didn’t actually lose a lot of data (went from 8436 to 8254 observations). Just to check that these interpolated tracks are similar to the original, let’s do a comparison on a few of them! real will be dark green, interpolated purple

#34501_2
int_34501_2 <- interp_df %>% dplyr::filter(ID == '34501_2')
real_34501_2 <- dat %>% dplyr::filter(tag == '34501') %>% dplyr::filter(track == 2)

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = int_34501_2, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'purple')+
  geom_point(data = real_34501_2, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'darkgreen', inherit.aes = F)+
  theme_classic()

#34507_31
int_34507_31 <- interp_df %>% dplyr::filter(ID == '34507_31')
real_34507_31 <- dat %>% dplyr::filter(tag == '34507') %>% dplyr::filter(track == 31)

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = int_34507_31, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'purple')+
  geom_point(data = real_34507_31, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'darkgreen', inherit.aes = F)+
  theme_classic()

#34518_12
int_34518_12 <- interp_df %>% dplyr::filter(ID == '34518_12')
real_34518_12 <- dat %>% dplyr::filter(tag == '34518') %>% dplyr::filter(track == 12)

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = int_34518_12, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'purple')+
  geom_point(data = real_34518_12, aes(x = x, y = y), color = 'darkgreen', inherit.aes = F)+
  theme_classic()

Filtering track by amount of time in the array

They match pretty well! Now comes the fourth big decision. What tracks are worth keeping in the array? Is a 5 minute track worth it? Probably not because it will only include 5 positions. But, you don’t want to get rid of too much data. For this study, we decided to cut it off at 30 minutes or longer in the array for each track. This represents a good amount of time where we might see two types of behaviors. So let’s filter some more!

id20 <- interp_df %>% group_by(ID) %>% mutate(tott = max(ts)-min(ts)) %>% ungroup()
id20$tottime <- as.numeric(id20$tott)
id20_30 <- id20 %>% dplyr::filter(tottime >= 1800)
nrow(as.data.frame(unique(id20_30$ID))) #number of unique tracks kept through all of the filtering - 59
## [1] 59

Prepping the data for HMMs

interp_df_30 <- id20_30 %>% arrange(ID, ts)
# prepData: coordinate names are "x" and "y" in our frame
hmm_data_30 <- prepData(interp_df_30, type = "UTM", coordNames = c("x", "y"))

# moveHMM uses a column 'step' and 'angle' (radians) created by prepData
# Remove rows with zero or NA step (stay/missing movement) because gamma requires positive steps
hmm_data_30 <- hmm_data_30 %>% filter(!is.na(step) & step > 0) %>% filter(!is.na(angle))

hmm_data_30 <- hmm_data_30 %>%
  filter(is.finite(step), is.finite(angle), step > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    step = pmax(step, quantile(step, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)),
    step = pmin(step, quantile(step, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))
  )

Determining the initial step lengths and turn angles for the model

We have prepped our data. However, it is still not just plug and play. We need to investigate our data to fit general curves to our data to inform the model. We don’t need to do this, but it creates a more informed model based on the original data. We are trying to fit these data into two behavioral states, so we will want to inform the model with 2 curves.

hist(hmm_data_30$step, breaks = 20, freq = F, main = "Step lengths")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.5, rate=0.9), n=200, add=TRUE, col="royalblue", lwd=4) #shape is how right-skewed the gamma curve is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.9, rate=0.7), n=200, add=TRUE, col="cadetblue", lwd=4) #rate is how tall the curve apex is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 2.2, rate=0.4), n=200, add=TRUE, col="navyblue", lwd=4)

#assign initial step length distributions
sl_init_mean <- c(2.2/0.4, 1.5/0.9) #initial means should be the shape/rate for both
sl_init_sd <- c(sqrt(2.2)/0.7, sqrt(1.5)/0.9) #initial standard deviations should be square root of shape/rate

This is a little subjective, but there is a good starting out point. The first curve encompasses the lower step lengths well. The second curve does not really add any more information either than including the step lengths that are longer. However, the third curve does this but also includes the higher amount of longer steps. So let’s go with the first and third curves

Now we do the same thing for the turn angles. However, we want the model to try to find states with opposite turn angles (turn 180 degrees vs straight). Therefore, we will play with the numbers a little.

hist(hmm_data_30$angle, breaks = 30, freq = F, main = "Turn angles")
curve(circular::dvonmises(x, mu = pi, kappa = 0.01), n=200, add=TRUE, col="royalblue", lwd=4) #mu is the mean direction of the angle
## Warning in as.circular(x): an object is coerced to the class 'circular' using default value for the following components:
##   type: 'angles'
##   units: 'radians'
##   template: 'none'
##   modulo: 'asis'
##   zero: 0
##   rotation: 'counter'
## conversion.circularxradians0counter
## Warning in as.circular(x): an object is coerced to the class 'circular' using default value for the following components:
##   type: 'angles'
##   units: 'radians'
##   template: 'none'
##   modulo: 'asis'
##   zero: 0
##   rotation: 'counter'
## conversion.circularmuradians0counter
curve(circular::dvonmises(x, mu = -0.1, kappa = 7), n=200, add=TRUE, col="cadetblue", lwd=4) #kappa is the concentration (how tall it is)
## Warning in as.circular(x): an object is coerced to the class 'circular' using default value for the following components:
##   type: 'angles'
##   units: 'radians'
##   template: 'none'
##   modulo: 'asis'
##   zero: 0
##   rotation: 'counter'
## conversion.circularxradians0counter
## Warning in as.circular(x): an object is coerced to the class 'circular' using default value for the following components:
##   type: 'angles'
##   units: 'radians'
##   template: 'none'
##   modulo: 'asis'
##   zero: 0
##   rotation: 'counter'
## conversion.circularmuradians0counter

#assign initial angle distributions
ta_init_mean <- c(-0.1, pi) #mean is from mu
ta_init_con <- c(7, 0.01) #concentration is kappa

The first curve is almost a straight line. But we want the model to try to fit 180 degree turn and straight. The second curve is straight ahead and the first is the turn around. It needs to be as close to flat as possible to fit the data the best.

Running HMMs

mod <- fitHMM(data = hmm_data_30,
               nbStates = 2,
               stepPar0 = c(sl_init_mean, sl_init_sd),
               anglePar0 = c(ta_init_mean, ta_init_con),
               formula = ~1)
## Warning in nlm(f = nLogLike, p = wpar, nbStates = nbStates, bounds = bounds, :
## NA/NaN replaced by maximum positive value
## Warning in nlm(f = nLogLike, p = wpar, nbStates = nbStates, bounds = bounds, :
## NA/NaN replaced by maximum positive value

mod

mod %>% plotPR() #gives the goodness of fit. Looks pretty good!
## Computing pseudo-residuals... DONE

Looking at the step length and angle distributions, you can see a few things. State 1 is categorized by longer step lengths (average of 4 meters) and straight turn angles (0.007 radians, basically zero). State 2, on the other hand, has a much shorter step length (average of 0.9 meters) but a similar turn angle (-0.02 radians). However, the concentration is a lot lower, so state 2 encompasses the larger turn angles. These results also give you a transistion probability to transition between states. Pretty low for both, but it does happen. If you run the following code, you can visualize the distributions for each state as well as which state each step on all the tracks is! Since that is 59 tracks, we won’t run it online but we will go through it in the workshop

# statecol <- c('lightblue', 'purple1')
# plot(mod, col = statecol)

##Now we can assign states directly to the dataframe

states <- viterbi(mod)

state_30 <- mod$data %>%
  mutate(state = states)

# Convert angle to degrees for interpretability (angles are in radians)
state_30 <- state_30 %>%
  mutate(angle_deg = angle * 180 / pi,
         abs_angle_deg = abs(angle_deg))

output_HMM_df <- state_30 %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, track, tag, ts, x, y, step, angle, angle_deg, state)

We have our final HMM dataset! Now we can move onto looking at what environmental variables we can use to model against the HMMs and for the iSSFs!
